# Test Setup and Evaluation

## Evaluation Framework

Because no ground truth labels are available, evaluation relies on internal validation
metrics, bootstrap stability, and interpretability rather than external criteria.

### Internal Validation Metrics

Three internal criteria are used to assess cluster quality across all methods. The
**average silhouette width** [@kaufman1990finding] measures how similar each observation
is to its own cluster relative to the nearest competing cluster, with higher values
indicating stronger separation and better-defined structure. The
**Calinski--Harabasz (CH) index** measures the ratio of between-cluster to
within-cluster scatter, where larger values indicate more compact and well-separated
clusters. For the probabilistic methods (PD and FPDC), a **probability silhouette** is
additionally computed using `Silh()` from the `FPDclustering` package
[@tortora2024fpdclustering], which extends the silhouette concept to soft membership
weights and is better suited to evaluating solutions where observations belong
partially to multiple clusters. For k-means only, **total within-cluster sum of squares
(WSS)** is also reported as it directly reflects the k-means objective and is used in
the elbow method for cluster count selection.

### Stability

Clustering algorithms such as k-means and RKM are sensitive to initialization and local
optima, so a method that yields highly variable solutions across repeated runs may be
unreliable even if its internal metrics appear strong in a single run
[@everitt2011cluster]. Bootstrap stability is therefore assessed for each method by
resampling 30% of users across 15 replicates and comparing each replicate's partition
to the full-data reference solution using the adjusted Rand index (ARI)
[@kaufman1990finding]. ARI ranges from 0 (no agreement beyond chance) to 1 (perfect
agreement), with higher values indicating more reproducible clustering solutions. For PD
and FPDC, hard labels are obtained by assigning each user to their highest-probability
cluster before computing ARI, enabling direct comparison across all four methods on a
common scale.

### Implementation Summary

All methods were applied to standardized embedding matrices of dimensions 64, 128, and
256. For each method, the number of clusters $k$ was selected primarily using the
highest average silhouette width, with the CH index used as a secondary criterion where
silhouette scores were tied or ambiguous. Where relevant, the reduced dimension $q$ was
selected jointly with $k$ over a two-dimensional grid. Intermediate results were cached
to `.rds` files to support reproducibility without rerunning the full pipeline during
rendering. The tuning ranges and selection criteria for each method are summarized in
Table X.

| Method | $k$ range | $q$ range | Primary criterion | Secondary criterion |
|--------|-----------|-----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| K-Means | $2, \ldots, 20$ | --- | Silhouette | CH, WSS |
| Reduced K-Means | $2, \ldots, 10$ | $2, \ldots, 6$ | Silhouette | CH |
| PD Clustering | $2, \ldots, 5$ | --- | Silhouette | CH, prob. silhouette |
| FPDC | $2, \ldots, 8$ | $2, \ldots, 5$ | Silhouette | CH, prob. silhouette |

Table: Tuning ranges and model selection criteria for each clustering method.
